reply_text:
You're right about the category. A vertical assumes a market organised by industry, where you buy the healthcare software or the logistics software. Your offering cuts across that. It's about agent-run work in general, whatever the work is. Asking for a vertical is like asking what industry a phone is for.

I'd push back on "there's no software anymore", though. Your phone works because there's a bare-metal server behind it running Agency, Emacs, the futon stack and a fleet of agents. The software didn't go away. It went out of sight. That's where your pitch comes in: once the software is out of sight, so is what it did. From the phone, all you see is "done". The gap, provenance and effect-with-controls offerings are how you see the machinery again when you need to. "Don't need a computer, just a phone" is the benefit. "…and here's how you know what the agents behind the phone actually did" is the product.

Her question still points at a real need even with the wrong category. A reader wants one concrete case to hold onto. Businesses that sell across industries usually answer "who" with an example, not a market segment. You already have one: **you**. One person with a phone, a server and a team of agents, running a company, a research programme and your tax filings. That covers "who" (people working like this, or about to), "what" (keeping that setup honest) and "outcome" (you can trust what it reports), and it doesn't limit you to any one industry.

The homepage already starts with "I thought I was getting really good at agentic coding…", so it's halfway there. What it doesn't say yet is that the person telling the story is working from a phone.
